paragraphs: I've worked in Lamorinda long enough to recognize a Branagh home on sight, and 31 Sandy Court caught my attention the moment it came to market. The combination of a three-home cul-de-sac setting, a .65-acre lot with its own vineyard, and the kind of interior updates that actually hold up to scrutiny is genuinely rare at any price point in Orinda. When the listing came off the market after 32 days without a sale, I wanted to reach out.

Thirty-two days is close to the edge of the window where buyer psychology starts to shift, and in a home priced at $2,895,000, perception matters enormously. My read on what happened is that the listing had strong bones but left several of the most compelling parts of this property underexplored in how it was positioned and distributed. The Branagh pedigree, the private vineyard, the cul-de-sac setting, the primary suite with its fireplace and spa bath  -  these aren't just nice-to-have features, they are the reasons a buyer at this level chooses one home over another. A standard MLS approach tends to mention those details and move on. At this price, buyers need to feel them before they make the drive.

I've put together a packet that walks through what I believe contributed to the outcome, how this home compares to the Orinda market right now, and what a relaunch strategy built specifically for 31 Sandy Court could look like. It's not a pitch for a lower price  -  it's a blueprint for reaching the buyers who are genuinely right for this home.

If you're already working with a real estate agent toward a new listing, please consider this a professional courtesy and feel free to set it aside. If you're not, I'd welcome a conversation whenever the timing feels right for you  -  no pressure, just a chance to look at the numbers together.

exec_summary.headline: A Branagh-Built Retreat on a Private Cul-de-Sac  -  and a Listing That Left the Best Parts Untold
exec_summary.p1: 31 Sandy Court has the fundamentals that Orinda buyers at the $2.9 million level are specifically looking for. A Branagh Development build signals quality before anyone walks through the door. The .65-acre lot, vineyard, hot tub, and expansive turf give the outdoor spaces a resort quality that is genuinely uncommon. Inside, soaring ceilings, a chef's kitchen open to the family room, a primary suite with a fireplace, and a spa-like renovated primary bath deliver the kind of lifestyle that justifies a premium  -  engineered hardwood, updated glass stair railings, and a dedicated office round out a home that is fully ready for a family to move in and not think twice.
exec_summary.p2: The listing history doesn't reflect a problem with the home. It reflects a strategy that treated a distinctive property like a standard inventory listing. At 32 days on market without a sale, this home was approaching the point where buyer hesitation becomes self-reinforcing. The Branagh name, the private vineyard, the cul-de-sac privacy, and the spa-caliber primary suite were all mentioned in the listing description  -  but in a market where buyers researching $2.9 million homes are comparing obsessively online before they ever schedule a showing, mentioning these features is not the same as selling them. The distribution and the media didn't build the case that the home itself absolutely supports.
exec_summary.p3: A relaunch for 31 Sandy Court needs to do one thing above all else: give the right buyer the visual and narrative depth to understand what makes this property singular before they visit. The Branagh pedigree, the private outdoor living environment, and the cul-de-sac setting are not features  -  they are the story. The strategy needs to lead with that story and put it in front of the specific buyers who are actively looking for it.

forensics.title: Friction #1: The Branagh Premium Was Named, Not Sold
forensics.body: At $865/sqft, 31 Sandy Court sits squarely in the architectural tier of the Orinda market, where buyers expect to understand exactly what they are paying for relative to other options. The listing description acknowledged the Branagh pedigree and the home's quality in general terms, but buyers comparing carefully at this price point need more than a name drop. The refined millwork, soaring ceilings, and spa-caliber primary suite are the specific reasons this home commands a premium over a standard updated Orinda listing  -  and each of those details deserved its own visual and narrative treatment. Without that depth, a well-informed buyer shopping $2.9 million in Orinda will second-guess the number rather than feel confident in it.
forensics.brightwork_contrast: BrightWork's 3D Matterport tour lets buyers walk through every detail of a home like this from anywhere, on their own time  -  so the millwork, the ceiling volumes, and the primary suite aren't described, they're experienced. Buyers who've already walked the home virtually arrive at showings ready to decide.

forensics.title: Friction #2: The Outdoor Story Was Undersold at a Critical Price Point
forensics.body: A private vineyard, a hot tub, entertaining patios, and a half-acre-plus of usable turf on a cul-de-sac lot are not features you find in standard Orinda inventory. These outdoor spaces are a primary reason a buyer chooses 31 Sandy Court over a comparable home on a smaller or more exposed lot  -  but standard ground photography and MLS listing angles rarely capture scale, setting, or the sense of privacy that makes a lot like this feel special. A buyer browsing online cannot tell the difference between a .65-acre sanctuary and a .35-acre backyard from a handful of ground-level photos. The lot's position at the end of a three-home cul-de-sac, the vineyard rows, the entertaining flow  -  these need to be shown, not summarized.
forensics.brightwork_contrast: BrightWork's Sky Tour uses aerial video to show lot position, setting, and the privacy of a home's placement in a way no ground photo can replicate  -  buyers see the scale of the vineyard, the cul-de-sac buffer, and the overall outdoor environment before they ever visit.

forensics.title: Friction #3: The Right Buyers Weren't Being Actively Found
forensics.body: A $2,895,000 home in Orinda has a specific buyer profile  -  often a SF or East Bay professional or family that is actively researching Lamorinda before committing to a showing schedule, comparing schools, commute access, and lifestyle carefully. At 32 days on market without a sale, the distribution strategy was working on a passive model: get on the MLS and major portals, and wait for the right buyer to find it. In a market where the qualifying buyer pool at this price point is finite and highly informed, passive distribution is a narrow path. The buyers who were genuinely right for 31 Sandy Court  -  drawn by the Branagh quality, the outdoor spaces, the top-rated schools, and the BART proximity  -  needed to be reached where they are actively researching, not just encountered if they happened across the listing.

positioning_table.verdict: At $865/sqft versus a benchmark range of $860-$950/sqft, this home sits near the lower end of that range. At $865/sqft, 31 Sandy Court is priced at the entry point of Orinda's architectural tier  -  a number this home's Branagh pedigree, oversized private lot, and renovated interiors genuinely support. The positioning is sound, but the strategy needed to do more work to close the gap between what the data says and what online buyers could actually see and feel. A relaunch that leads with the outdoor setting, the builder quality, and the depth of the interior updates puts the marketing in line with what the home is already delivering.

pillars.title: Pillar I  -  Build the Visual Case Before the First Showing
pillars.body: A Branagh home with a private vineyard, soaring ceilings, and a spa-caliber primary suite is not a property that photographs like standard Orinda inventory  -  and it shouldn't be marketed like it. The visual package for 31 Sandy Court needs to capture scale, light, and the quality of the build in a way that gives online buyers the confidence to schedule a showing rather than move on to the next listing. BrightWork's Sky Tour and 3D Matterport give buyers the aerial perspective on the lot and the interior walkthrough that standard photography simply doesn't deliver. Buyers who arrive having already experienced the home are buyers who are ready to move.

pillars.title: Pillar II  -  Reach the Buyer Before They Find Something Else
pillars.body: The buyers who are right for 31 Sandy Court are not waiting to stumble across it on the MLS. They are professionals and families in San Francisco and the East Bay who are actively researching Orinda right now  -  comparing commute times to BART, reviewing school ratings, and building a mental shortlist. BrightWork's geo-targeted digital campaigns put this home in front of those buyers while they are still in the research phase, before they have committed to another listing or another neighborhood. Passive distribution assumes the right buyer finds you. Active distribution makes sure they do.

pillars.title: Pillar III  -  Tell the Cul-de-Sac Story, Not Just the Square Footage
pillars.body: The privacy of a three-home cul-de-sac, the rhythm of a working vineyard, the hot tub at sunset, the turf for kids and dogs  -  these are the things a buyer at $2.9 million is actually buying, and they don't fit in a bullet point. The marketing for a relaunch of 31 Sandy Court needs to lead with the lifestyle and let the specifications follow. BrightWork's listing narrative and Zillow Showcase placement are built to tell that story where the most qualified buyers are already looking  -  turning a scroll into a click, and a click into a conversation.
